claims.claim: The thermodynamic minimum energy for desalinating seawater is around 1 kWh per cubic meter.
claims.episode_span: the thermodynamic minimum for separating salt or contaminants — about one kilowatt-hour per cubic meter for seawater, far less for brackish water
claims.supporting_quote: A minimum energy consumption for seawater desalination of around 1 kWh/m 3 has been determined

claims.claim: Real-world seawater desalination plants draw roughly 3 kWh per cubic meter (2018 global energy intensity), several times the thermodynamic minimum.
claims.episode_span: against the three to four that real reverse-osmosis plants draw — translating to a few cents more at industrial electricity rates
claims.supporting_quote: The energy intensity of seawater desalination has improved: It is now about 3 kWh/m 3 (in 2018), down by a factor of 10 from 20-30 kWh/m 3 in 1970.

claims.claim: Desalinating brackish water requires less energy than desalinating seawater.
claims.episode_span: about one kilowatt-hour per cubic meter for seawater, far less for brackish water
claims.supporting_quote: Brackish water desalination requires less energy than seawater desalination.

claims.claim: Delivered municipal water prices commonly run on the order of one to several dollars per cubic meter; a 310-city survey found an average combined water and wastewater tariff of US$1.98/m3.
claims.episode_span: The finished delivered cost in many municipal systems, by contrast, ranges from roughly one to several dollars per cubic meter once capital recovery, operations, and distribution are included.
claims.supporting_quote: Among the 310 cities in the GWI 2012 tariff survey the average combined water and wastewater tariff was US$1.98/m3 for the 15 m3/month

claims.claim: The buried distribution and transmission network, not treatment, dominates drinking-water infrastructure expense: EPA's 7th needs survey puts distribution/transmission needs at $422.9 billion versus $107 billion for treatment.
claims.episode_span: In many regions the buried network itself accounts for the majority of lifetime expense, turning what physics treats as a simple separation task into a decades-long infrastructure commitment.
claims.source_title: EPA's 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment | US EPA
claims.supporting_quote: Distribution and transmission: $422.9 billion to replace or rehabilitate aging or deteriorating pipelines and appurtenances. Treatment: $107 billion to construct, expand or rehabilitate infrastructure to reduce contamination.

claims.claim: US drinking-water systems face $625 billion in 20-year infrastructure needs, led by pipe replacement.
claims.episode_span: The overwhelming share of that multiplier lives downstream of the treatment plant.
claims.source_title: EPA's 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment | US EPA
claims.supporting_quote: The survey determined that drinking water systems will need $625 billion for pipe replacement, treatment plant upgrades, storage tanks, and other key assets

claims.claim: Distribution and transmission pipe accounts for $421 billion (67%) of US 20-year drinking-water infrastructure needs, versus $55.3 billion (17%) for treatment.
claims.episode_span: In many regions the buried network itself accounts for the majority of lifetime expense
claims.source_title: Drinking Water Infrastructure - ASCE 2025 Report Card for America's Infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: Water distribution and transmission infrastructure accounts for $421 billion (67%) of total future needs, followed by treatment needs accounting for 55.3 billion (17%).

claims.claim: US drinking-water infrastructure comprises more than 2 million miles of buried transmission and distribution lines; the oldest date to the 19th century and post-WWII pipe lasts 75-100 years.
claims.episode_span: a shared, buried, capital-intensive network whose design assumptions have changed little since the early twentieth century
claims.source_title: Drinking Water Infrastructure - ASCE 2025 Report Card for America's Infrastructure
claims.supporting_quote: Drinking water infrastructure in the U.S. comprises more than 2 million miles of underground transmission and distribution lines. Some of the nation’s oldest pipes were laid in the 19th century, and pipes laid post–World War II have an average lifespan of 75 to 100 years

claims.claim: AWWA's Buried No Longer study put buried drinking-water pipe investment needs at more than $1 trillion over 2011-2035 if pipes are replaced at end of life.
claims.episode_span: turning what physics treats as a simple separation task into a decades-long infrastructure commitment
claims.source_title: Water Infrastructure Bill To Top $1 Trillion - Water Online
claims.supporting_quote: Investment needs for buried drinking water infrastructure total more than $1 trillion nationwide over the next 25 years (between 2011 and 2035), if pipes are replaced at the end of their useful lives.

claims.claim: Water systems built in the late 19th and 20th centuries have mostly never yet faced large-scale pipe replacement — the legacy network is a century-old design commitment.
claims.episode_span: Once the pipe is in the ground, every joint, valve, and meter must be inspected and replaced on schedules set by regulators
claims.source_title: Water Infrastructure Bill To Top $1 Trillion - Water Online
claims.supporting_quote: Because pipe assets last a long time, water systems that were built in the latter part of the 19th century and throughout much of the 20th century have, for the most part, never experienced the need for pipe replacement on a large scale
